name: PT Janu Putra Sejahtera Tbk.

frontmatter.title: Janu Putra Sejahtera: a poultry recovery that belongs to the asset buyer, not the shareholder
frontmatter.summary: AYAM has swung from a nine-month loss to a profit, but the profit is dominated by the gain on the sale and leaseback of its own farms, not by a margin recovery: the third quarter earned under one per cent gross margin. At witnessed poultry economics the enterprise is worth a fraction of its book value, and the market capitalisation prices a franchise the company does not have.
thesis: The swing to profit is an asset-sale gain, not operating leverage: net other income exceeded gross profit, and the exit-quarter gross margin was under one per cent.

Poultry economics are hostile and AYAM is a price-taker: farm-gate live birds trade below independent producers' cost of production, and the company sells feed-cost-exposed product into a domestic market it does not set.
The sale and leaseback of land, buildings and plant converts an owned asset base into a rent obligation, cutting depreciation and raising operating cost, and the lease terms are not disclosed.
The discounted cash flow is small against a market capitalisation that is a large multiple of book equity, and even the asset-sale consideration in the equity bridge does not close the gap.
The bull case is government supply discipline lifting live-bird prices and chick demand compounding, and even that case leaves the shares far above our value.

catalysts.event: Monthly farm-gate live-bird and feed price surveys we track
FY2026 audited accounts: the split between the disposal gain and operating profit
First full year of lease payments on the sold farms
Parent-stock culling decisions and chick supply policy for the next cycle

blocks.text: We initiate on PT Janu Putra Sejahtera at **SELL** with a twelve-month target of **Rp20**, a return of -95.8% from the Rp484 close [S0]. The company is a small integrated poultry producer - parent-stock breeding, day-old chicks, commercial broilers, table eggs and a slaughterhouse - selling only into the domestic market [S6]. The shares have re-rated violently: the market capitalisation is IDR1,936.0bn, more than eight times the September book value of 226 IDR bn, and the stock trades at many times the book value of a business whose return on that book has been close to nothing [S0].

The variant view is simple, and it is not a cautious one. The market is paying for a turnaround that has happened in the headline and has not happened in the business. The nine months to September produced a net profit of 17.6 IDR bn on sales of 203 IDR bn, but net other income of 20.0 IDR bn - most of it the gain on the sale and leaseback of the company's own farms - was larger than the entire gross profit of 10.6 IDR bn [S3]. Strip that out and the operating result was close to breakeven on a nine-month average that a single strong first quarter flatters: the second quarter earned about one per cent and the third under one per cent [S0]. The industry the company sells into has farm-gate live birds at 17,000 IDR per kg per kilogram against an independent producer's cost of production of 22,500 IDR per kg, a loss per kilogram that has persisted for weeks [S7].

What moves the value is therefore not demand. It is three things. First, whether live-bird and chick prices recover above cost, which is a policy question as much as a market one [S9]. Second, what rent the company now pays for the farms it no longer owns, because the lease was signed the same day the assets were transferred and the terms are not in the public disclosure [S8]. Third, whether the layer capacity the company is putting money into earns a return rather than adding to an already oversupplied market [S6]. Our base case is a cycle that recovers from the trough to 5.0% by FY2030E - below every year the company earned before the downturn - and the value that produces is Rp20 a share.

We are deliberately not taking the most cautious path, and the way we avoid it is by anchoring on what the company actually reported. The nine months produced gross profit of 10.6 IDR bn on sales of 203 IDR bn, a margin of about five per cent [S3, F19, F20], and we carry the fourth quarter at the rate just reported rather than at that nine-month average, so the full year realises 4.2% with the December quarter at about one per cent. The second and third quarters were a trough at about one per cent [S0], and we do not extrapolate the trough any more than we extrapolate the first quarter. The chick business is genuinely growing and the cost of sales fell faster than sales, which is why the base case returns to the mid-cycle margin by FY2030E instead of staying at the run-rate. Even so, the value that produces is Rp20 against a price of Rp484, which is the whole of the call: the operating improvement is real but small, and the price already assumes a franchise the company has not built.

Poultry in Indonesia is a commodity business with a long history of boom and bust. Breeders and
integrators make money when the national flock is short and lose it when everyone expands at once.
The product is perishable, the price is set daily at the farm gate, and the smallest producers carry
the least bargaining power with feed suppliers and buyers. A company without its own feed mill buys
the most expensive part of its cost base at retail and sells its output at wholesale. That is the
structural position here, and it is why we weight operating economics far above headline earnings
and why a re-rating of the shares does not, by itself, change what the business is worth.

AYAM is a vertically integrated poultry producer built around four revenue lines: commercial broiler sales from its own farms, day-old chicks from parent-stock breeding and hatchery operations, table eggs from layer farms, and chicken carcasses plus tolling services through its slaughterhouse [S6]. The company describes its purpose as poultry farming, poultry slaughtering and packing, and livestock supporting services, and it serves the domestic market only [S6]. It listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in November 2023 and had 4,000 m shares shares outstanding at the end of FY2025 [S6, F38]. It employed 311 people people at that date, down from the prior year as the cost programme ran through the organisation [S6, F39].

The revenue mix has inverted, and that is the single most important operating fact about the company. In FY2025 commercial broiler sales were 136 IDR bn, day-old chicks 107 IDR bn, eggs 23.6 IDR bn and carcasses and tolling 0.8 IDR bn [S6, F25-F28]. A year earlier the broiler line was more than twice the chick line; by FY2025 the two had almost crossed, and by the nine months of 2026 the chick line was 144 IDR bn of revenue after growing by more than four-fifths year on year [S3, F23]. The broiler business, which was the core of the company at listing, has shrunk to a minority of sales.

The economics of that shift are different in kind. A broiler is a commodity sold by weight into a market where the farm-gate price is set by supply and demand and where independent producers currently lose money on every kilogram [S7, F29, F30]. A day-old chick is a breeder product sold to other farmers who intend to raise it; its price tracks the cost of the parent-stock operation and the appetite of the downstream flock, and its volume is directly exposed to government supply management, which culls productive parent stock early to control the number of chicks reaching the market [S9, F41]. Being a chick seller therefore means holding a policy-sensitive volume and a cost-linked price, which is a better position than being a live-bird seller but not a moat.

The production chain runs from parent-stock farms, through a hatchery, into broiler and layer farms, and out through a slaughterhouse that also takes tolling work [S6]. The company also holds a fifth of an associate, PT Janu Putra Abadi [S6, F40], whose profit share arrives in other income rather than in the operating line, and whose contribution has been volatile.

The ownership of that chain changed materially in the middle of 2026. On 29 July the company transferred fifteen land plots totalling 129,645 sqm square metres, the buildings standing on them, and the plant and equipment that supports operations, to PT Universal Agri Bisnisindo for 70.0 IDR bn, equal to 33.5% of FY2025 equity, and signed a lease agreement over the same assets on the same day so that it keeps using them [S8, F35-F37]. The company presents the transaction as providing flexibility in asset and funding management. The economic substance is a sale and leaseback: the company has converted owned capacity into a consideration and a rent obligation, which lowers depreciation and raises operating cost, and which fixes a claim on its cash flow ahead of shareholders. The disclosure states the consideration but not how it was settled - cash or an offset - nor the rent, so both are analysed from the balance sheet rather than assumed [S8].

Strategically the company is a challenger in every sense. It is a single-province producer selling into a domestic market with no consumer brand and no export channel, and a balance sheet that has been financed by supplier credit and bank debt rather than by equity [S0, S6]. We find no disclosure of feed milling of its own in the material we hold, and its own cost discussion is about the price of purchased feed inputs rather than a milling margin [S6, S7]; the cost-link shares in our model are our own estimates for that reason. Its scale is a fraction of the integrated groups it competes with. The investment case does not rest on it becoming an integrator; it rests on whether a small breeder can earn a return in a market that is oversupplied and administratively managed.

The national poultry complex is in oversupply, and the price evidence is unambiguous. Independent producers report farm-gate live-bird prices of 17,000 IDR per kg per kilogram against a cost of production of 22,500 IDR per kg, a loss of several thousand rupiah on every kilogram sold, and they say the condition has persisted for almost three weeks [S7, F29, F30]. The cost stack behind that number is feed at 10,000 IDR per kg per kilogram, feed-grade corn at 7,800 IDR per kg, imported soybean meal at 10,000 IDR per kg, and day-old chicks above 8,800 IDR per bird a bird [S7, F31-F34]. Producers are asking government to cut the cost of raw materials, to enforce the reference purchase price against slaughterhouses and brokers, and to direct integrator volume away from traditional markets [S7].

Policy is the swing factor in this industry, not the weather and not the consumer. The breeders' association, of which AYAM is a member [S6], describes a system in which government manages chick supply by culling productive parent stock early - at fifty to fifty-five weeks against a normal laying life of 65.0 weeks - and in which producers are told not to price too high during the festive season nor too low afterwards [S9, F41]. A corn support programme runs alongside it [S9]. The association's concern is that supply control sits awkwardly with competition law, which is why it is arguing for the rules to be synchronised as the competition statute is revised [S9]. For a chick seller, that is a policy-set volume. For a live-bird seller, it is a policy-influenced price. Neither is a market the company controls.

Our sector deck prices the two inputs that dominate cost, corn and soybean meal, and both are forecast above spot. That matters more here than in most consumer names because the margin is single-digit: a feed-cost rise of the size the deck carries is most of the profit, and the company has no pricing power to offset it. The evidence for that absence of pricing power is in the company's own segment disclosure, where broiler revenue collapsed while chick revenue grew [S6, F25, F26]. That is what a price-taker's mix looks like when it chases the one product that still has demand.

Competitive positioning is weak and we do not dress it up. Market share is not disclosed by the company and no industry body publishes a share for a producer of this size, so we cannot size it against the national flock [S6]. On the five forces: supplier power is high, because feed and corn are concentrated and policy-priced; buyer power is high, because integrators, traders and slaughterhouses set the farm-gate price; the threat of entry is high at the smallholder end where capital requirements are modest; substitutes are weak in the abstract but irrelevant at these margins; and rivalry is severe because the product is undifferentiated and perishable. The only candidate moat is breeding stock and hatchery capacity, and it is not exclusive: the association's own membership is a list of breeders [S9].

External influences run through three channels. The first is the rupiah, because soybean meal is imported and priced in dollars; the macro deck's exchange-rate path feeds straight into the cost link in our model [S0]. The second is agricultural policy on corn, which determines whether feed cost tracks the world market or a domestic administered price [S9]. The third is the supply management regime itself, which can lift prices by culling or crush them by allowing expansion [S9, F41]. None of these is within the company's control, and all three dominate its margin.

The five-year record is a business that shrank and then stabilised at a much lower level of profitability. Revenue was IDR395.6bn in FY2022, IDR352.3bn in FY2023, IDR361.3bn in FY2024 and IDR267.1bn in FY2025 [S0, S6]. Cost of sales took IDR258.2bn of the latest year, leaving gross profit of IDR8.9bn, a gross margin of 3.3% against 5.7% a year earlier [S6]. Operating expenses of IDR13.6bn then produced an operating loss of IDR-4.0bn [S6, F7], and the year reached net profit of only IDR0.1bn because other income and the associate's share covered the shortfall [S6, F15]. The FY2025 result is, in substance, a nil year.

Two data-pack lines are wrong and we restate both. Depreciation charged in FY2025 was IDR6.0bn - depreciation in cost of sales plus depreciation in general and administrative expense - and not the fraction the pack carries, because the cash-flow statement is prepared on the direct method and has no depreciation add-back line [S6, F9]. The FY2024 charge was IDR7.5bn [S6, F10]. We also restate the operating result to the figure the income statement reports, which differs from the pack in both years [S6, F7, F8]. The effect is to lift FY2025 EBITDA to IDR1.9bn and to make the cash cost of production visible rather than flattered: at the pack's depreciation the business looks as though it barely uses capital, which is the opposite of the truth for a breeder with farms, cages and hatcheries.

Cash generation is thin. Operating cash flow was -26.4 IDR bn in FY2024, because working capital absorbed cash as inventory and receivables built, and recovered to 4.7 IDR bn in FY2025 as the company ran the balance sheet down [S6, F13, F14]. Capex has been negligible at IDR1.7bn in FY2025 [S6, F11], which is itself a signal: a business that stopped investing because it could not earn a return on new capacity. Working capital is trade-financed, with inventory and payables of similar magnitude against a modest revenue base, and the company relies on supplier credit rather than equity to fund the flock [S0].

The balance sheet carries the risk. Net debt was IDR40.2bn at the FY2025 year-end [S0], against an equity base of IDR208.8bn at the same date [S0], and the data pack's latest balance sheet, 30 June 2026, carries a larger net debt figure struck on the pre-transaction debt and minimal cash [S0]. Finance expenses of IDR4.4bn in FY2025 consumed more than the whole operating result [S6, F17]. A company with a gross margin in the low single digits and an interest bill of that size has almost no room to absorb a bad year, which is why the sale and leaseback was necessary and why it is not costless.

The nine-month actual changes the shape of the current year without changing its quality. Sales of 203 IDR bn were down on the prior year, but cost of sales fell faster, and gross profit of 10.6 IDR bn replaced a gross loss [S3, F20, F42]. Then 20.0 IDR bn of net other income - the disposal gain - carried pre-tax profit to a level the operating business did not earn [S3, F22]. Net profit of 17.6 IDR bn and equity of 226 IDR bn at the end of September are the numbers the market is looking at; the operating line underneath them is the number that matters [S3].

Our forecast reflects that split. Revenue is IDR278.3bn this year, IDR300.5bn next year and IDR357.9bn by the end of the explicit period, growing at the rates in the assumption table [S3]. The realised gross margin is not held at the nine-month average, which a single strong first quarter flatters: it is 4.2% this year - the actual nine months plus a fourth quarter at the rate the third quarter just reported - 3.0% next year at the exit run-rate, and then a recovery to 5.0% by FY2030E as the cycle normalises to a level below every year the company earned before the downturn [S0, S3]. From FY2031E the realised margin steps to 6.5% and eases to 4.5% by FY2035E, because the deck's corn and soymeal curves keep rising while only part of the cost passes into selling prices; that step is an artefact of the model's long-run input being re-set once, not a forecast of better trading, and we disclose it rather than leave it in the terminal value. Other non-operating income is IDR22.0bn this year, most of it the disposal gain, and a normal run-rate thereafter [S3, S8]. Operating cost is set at the rate the nine-month accounts imply once the other income is stripped out, lifted by the rent that the leaseback now requires [S8]. Capex is held at the rate the company actually spent, because the land and buildings it uses are no longer its own to buy [S6, F11, S8].

Earnings quality is the central analytical issue and we run the method card on it explicitly. The accruals pattern is adverse: profit has repeatedly run ahead of operating cash, and the one year in our forecast with a headline profit is dominated by a disposal gain rather than by operations [S3, S6]. Inventory has outgrown cost of sales as the flock and feed stocks were carried through the downturn, and working capital is financed by supplier credit [S0]. None of this is manipulation-class: the disclosure is clear, the related-party transaction was announced, and the auditor issued a clean opinion [S6]. It is optics-class in the precise sense the card defines - headline earnings overstate the earning power of the business - and our valuation does not capitalise the gain.

We use a discounted cash flow as the primary method because the value of this company is the cash its assets produce, and because the alternatives fail on their own terms: the earnings base is negative in the last audited year and the peer set is a group of integrated producers whose margins AYAM does not share [S0, S6]. The cost of equity is built from a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium, a country risk premium for Indonesia and an industry beta of 90.0% unlevered, levered to 91.9% for the company's gearing [S0]. The result is a cost of equity of 12.0% and, after the debt weight and the after-tax cost of debt, a weighted average cost of capital of 11.9%, inside the house band for rupiah names [S0]. Terminal growth is 4.0%, below long-run nominal GDP for the country, which is the discipline the compounder card requires of a domestic-only producer [S0].

The explicit forecast and the terminal value together produce an enterprise value of IDR26.8bn [S0]. The bridge from that to equity is where this company is misread, so we set it out line by line. The balance sheet the data pack carries is 30 June 2026, and the net debt the bridge deducts is the net debt on that balance sheet, struck as the pack's total debt less its cash and bank balances at that date [S0] - the line the discounted-cash-flow table prints directly above. It is not the smaller FY2025 year-end figure of IDR40.2bn [S0], which predates both the half-year and the transaction and which a reader substituting it would turn into a smaller deduction and a value too high [S0]. On 29 July 2026 the company transferred land, buildings and plant to PT Universal Agri Bisnisindo for a consideration of 70.0 IDR bn, leased back the same day [S8, F35, F37]. That consideration reduces net debt by its full amount whichever way it was settled: cash raises cash, and an offset against the buyer retires debt. It is therefore carried as a bridge item at full probability, separate from the P&L gain that sits in other non-operating income below EBIT and so cannot be reached twice by a cash-flow valuation. The 30 September balance sheet confirms the reading: total assets of 496 IDR bn against 510 IDR bn at the prior year-end, total liabilities of 270 IDR bn against 302 IDR bn, and equity of 226 IDR bn against 209 IDR bn [S3, F44-F48]. Assets fell while equity rose by the nine-month profit because the consideration went to liabilities and to the book value of the assets transferred. With the associate stake already carried in the pack's investments line, that bridge leaves a value of Rp15 a share before the cross-checks and a blended value of Rp15 a share [S0]. Terminal value is 45.5% of the total, so the conclusion is not an artefact of the perpetuity: it is the operating cash flow, which is small because the margin is small, because the interest bill takes most of what is left, and because the rent now runs through operating cost [S6, S8].

The terminal value needs one caveat and we state it rather than bury it. In the final forecast year capital spending is held at the rate the company has actually spent [S6, F11], while depreciation is running above that rate, so the terminal free cash flow the perpetuity capitalises includes a slow run-off of the asset base and not maintenance reinvestment alone. Setting capex equal to depreciation in the terminal year would drive terminal free cash flow below zero and remove roughly a third of the base value per share. We disclose the effect instead of re-striking the base, because the under-investment is what the company has done for two years and the bear case is where we charge for it; the reader should treat the base value as the top of the operating range, not its centre.

The multiple-survival test is the reason we do not lean on comparables. On our terminal cash flow, the exit enterprise value implied by the discounted cash flow is a low single-digit multiple of EBITDA, well below the multiple the shares trade on today [S0]. A valuation that requires the exit multiple to exceed the entry multiple is multiple expansion wearing a discounted-cash-flow costume, and we name it rather than publish it.

The cross-checks diverge, and the divergence is diagnostic rather than embarrassing. We drop the P/E from the blend altogether rather than carry it at a token weight. The engine strikes multiples on last-twelve-month earnings, those earnings are the nil FY2025 year - IDR0.1bn [S6, F15] - and a multiple applied to a year that earned nothing returns almost nothing and is floored at zero, so the method can only ever push the value down: that is a floor dressed as a cross-check, which is what the method card warns against. The EV/EBITDA cross-check is struck on the same trough year's EBITDA and, once net debt is deducted and the disposal consideration added back, it produces Rp10 a share against the discounted cash flow's Rp15 [S0]. We explain that divergence rather than average it: the trough EBITDA capitalises a year in which working capital was being liquidated, while the cash flow carries the margin recovery, so neither number is wrong and the gap between them is the width of the uncertainty about the cycle.

The two assumptions carrying most of the value are the realised gross margin and the revenue path. A change of a percentage point in the gross margin moves the value per share by more than the whole value in some cells of the sensitivity grid, which tells you how little equity cushion sits above the debt: the enterprise value has to clear net debt before the shareholder receives anything, and the margin is the only lever large enough to do it [S0].

What the price implies is the cleanest statement of the mispricing. A reverse discounted cash flow at Rp484 does not bracket on any revenue growth we can justify, because the current capitalisation requires an enterprise value several times what the witnessed margin can service [S0, S3]. The market is not discounting this company's cash flows; it is pricing an option on a policy-driven recovery, and the option is expensive relative to the cash flow that would have to arrive to justify it.

One dating point, because it is the kind of small mechanical gap that compounds into a wrong answer. The target is the blended value per share rolled forward twelve months at the cost of equity from the 30 June 2026 valuation date the discounted cash flow discounts from, which is the house twelve-month convention. The price we quote is the 4 November 2026 close, so the two dates do not coincide; rolling the target to the price date instead would add about four months of discounting, a few per cent of value, and changes no conclusion. The per-share figures in this section are per-share values throughout, not equity totals.
The risks that matter, with our judgement of likelihood and impact:

items: **Poultry price cycle (high likelihood, high impact).** Farm-gate live birds trade below
independent producers' cost of production, and the condition has persisted for weeks [S7, F29,
F30]. The company cannot set its own selling price, so a prolonged trough passes straight through
to its margin.
**Feed cost (high, high).** Corn and soybean meal are forecast above spot in our sector deck, and
the cost links in our model pass only part of that through to selling prices [S7, F31-F33]. On a
single-digit gross margin, a feed move of the deck's size is most of the profit.
**Policy (medium, high).** Chick supply and parent-stock culling decisions are administrative
[S9, F41]. A change in the culling rule changes both the volume the company sells and the price it
gets, in the same direction at once.
**Lease and balance-sheet risk (medium, high).** After the sale and leaseback the company pays
rent on the assets it operates, out of a margin that barely covers depreciation, and net debt is
large relative to cash flow [S8, F35-F37]. The lease terms are not disclosed in the material we
hold, which is itself a risk: the base case charges rent equal to the depreciation the sale
removed, and a market rent at a normal yield on the consideration would be a multiple of that and
turns the operating line negative on its own. The bear case carries that market rent.
**Liquidity (medium, medium).** The free float is 23.5% and insiders hold
79.0% [S0], so the register is concentrated enough for the controlling
interest to determine a vote, and the three-month traded value of IDR12,526,451,958.1bn
is small against the market capitalisation. The balance-sheet side is tighter still: at the 30
June 2026 balance sheet current liabilities exceeded current assets, a current ratio below one,
with a large current-debt bill against minimal cash [S0]. A refinancing that is not rolled is a
live downside, and the bear case charges two points more for it.
**Governance (low, medium).** A related-party asset sale equal to a third of book equity, leased
back the same day, whose pricing and rent cannot be benchmarked from the disclosure we hold [S8,
**Execution (medium, medium).** The chick line is growing quickly off a small base and now
dominates revenue [S3, F23]; a policy-driven slowdown in chick demand would hit the one line that
is working.

blocks.text: Bear (25.0%) values the shares at Rp2: oversupply persists into the next cycle, the gross margin stays at the exit run-rate instead of converging on the FY2025 witnessed level, the undisclosed rent on the leased farms is charged at a market yield rather than at the depreciation it replaced, and refinancing costs two points more against a current ratio below one. Base (50.0%) is Rp15: the margin recovers from the trough to a mid-cycle level below every year the company earned before the downturn, revenue grows modestly and the disposal gain is not repeated. Bull (25.0%) is Rp49: supply discipline lifts live-bird prices back above cost of production, the gross margin returns to the top of the range the company earned in FY2022 to FY2024 and above it at the peak, chick demand compounds, the rent the leaseback now charges falls away as the sold assets are renegotiated, and refinancing is cheaper.

The bear and bull cases shock the same four drivers, but the rent leg is expressed as the rent itself rather than mirrored across the pair. The bear adds a market rent on the 70.0 IDR bn consideration, about two points of operating cost; the bull removes only the rent the base already charges, which is the depreciation the sale replaced [S6, F9, S8], so the bull does not collect free operating efficiency from the leaseback it is meant to be escaping. Revenue growth, gross margin and the cost of debt are mirrored, so the asymmetry in the outcomes comes from the operating leverage in a business with a thin margin, not from a stacked set of assumptions. Even the bull case does not reach today's price, which is the honest statement of the call: the shares are expensive in every scenario we can defend, they are simply less catastrophically expensive if supply discipline works.

Signposts that would change our view. First, two consecutive quarters of farm-gate prices above independent cost of production, which would tell us the culling regime is working [S7, F29, F30]. Second, audited accounts in which the operating line, not other income, carries the profit [S3]. Third, disclosure of the lease terms, which would let us size the rent claim properly [S8]. Fourth, evidence that the layer capacity is earning a return rather than adding to the national surplus [S6]. Any two of those together would justify revisiting the bear case; the first alone would justify revisiting the sector view, not the stock.

Control is concentrated. Insiders hold 79.0% of the shares and the free float is 23.5% [S0], so the controlling interest can determine the outcome of any shareholder vote. The board is led by a president commissioner and a president director, and the company maintains an audit committee, a nomination and remuneration committee, a corporate secretary, an internal audit unit and an internal control system, all described in the annual report [S6]. The auditor is Jonnardi, Jamaludin, Sukimto & Rekan, a member of Audittrust International, and the opinion on the FY2025 accounts is "fairly, in all material respects" - a clean opinion [S6].

The governance event of the year is the asset transfer. Fifteen land plots of 129,645 sqm square metres, with the buildings and plant on them, went to PT Universal Agri Bisnisindo for 70.0 IDR bn, or 33.5% of FY2025 equity, and the company signed a lease over the same assets the same day so that it could keep operating them [S8, F35-F37]. The disclosure explains the rationale as flexibility in asset and funding management and states that operations, legal position, finances and going concern are unaffected. We take the disclosure at face value and still flag two things: the transaction transfers a third of book equity to a counterparty whose identity and relationship to the company we cannot establish from the material we hold, and neither the sale price nor the rent is benchmarked against an independent valuation in the disclosure. That is the modal value-destruction channel on this exchange, and it is the first question the red team should press.

Related-party gravity more broadly: the company sells and buys within a group that includes an associate it owns a fifth of [S6, F40], and the associate's profit share has swung between a profit and a loss across the last two years [S6]. We have not found evidence of sales to or purchases from affiliates at scale in the material we hold, but we also cannot rule it out from the summary disclosures, and we say so rather than assert either way.

Dividends: none since listing, and none in our forecast [S0]. With a nil audited profit, a leveraged balance sheet and a capital programme, a distribution is not a realistic use of cash in the near term, and the absence of a dividend record is consistent with that.

On ESG, the material exposures are the ones that come with livestock: animal welfare and stocking density, biosecurity and disease control, antibiotic use in feed, water and waste management at scale, and the labour intensity of farm work in a business with 311 people employees [S6, F39]. The company reports certifications, publishes a sustainability report alongside its annual report, and describes community programmes [S6]. We have not found an enforcement action, a special notation or a suspension in the sources we hold, and we make no claim beyond that.

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter; each is tied to a disclosure we hold [S3, S7, S8, S9]. Between updates we watch a short list of variables, because the investment case turns on a handful of numbers.

The first is the farm-gate live-bird price against independent cost of production, from the producer surveys published through the financial press; the gap between those two numbers is the best single indicator of whether the industry is recovering [S7, F29, F30]. The second is the cost of feed: corn and soybean meal prices, and any change in the corn support programme, feed straight into the cost links in our model [S9, F32, F33]. The third is chick supply policy, since culling decisions change both the volume the company sells and the price it receives [S9, F41].

At the company level we watch three things. The quarterly split between operating profit and other income, which tells us whether the business or the balance sheet is producing the result [S3]. Lease payments and any further asset transfers, which tell us how much of the sale proceeds the company is paying back as rent [S8]. And the audited FY2026 accounts, which will separate the disposal gain from the operating year for the first time and give us a clean base for the next forecast [S3]. We will update the coverage when the full-year accounts are published, or earlier if the price of live birds moves decisively above cost.

bear.narrative: The market does not recover to mid-cycle. Fed by the oversupply the producers' association describes [S9, F41], the gross margin stays at the Q2-Q3 2026 exit run-rate of about 1 per cent rather than converging to the FY2025 witnessed level, so revenue growth is three points lower and the gross margin three points lower than base in every year. The undisclosed rent on the sale and leaseback is charged at a market yield of about 8 per cent of the Rp70bn consideration - Rp5.6bn a year, equal to a two-point opex uplift - instead of the depreciation it replaced [S8, F35], and refinancing the debt that falls due against a current ratio of 0.98 costs two points more [S0].

bull.narrative: The government's supply control bites - early culling of parent stock at 50-55 weeks against a normal 65 [S9, F41] - and the farm-gate live-bird price recovers above cost of production, with the chick line, now 70.78 per cent of revenue [S3, F23], compounding. Revenue growth is three points higher and the gross margin three points higher than base in every year: on the base path that is a realised margin of eight to nine and a half per cent at mid-cycle, above the 7.5 per cent of FY2022 and the 6.8 per cent of FY2023 [S0, S6] but well below the 16.6 per cent the first quarter of 2026 actually earned on Rp9.39bn of gross profit over Rp56.39bn of sales [S0]. The bull is a full peak-cycle recovery, not an extrapolation of the March spike. The rent leg is expressed as the rent itself and not as a mirror of the bear: base charges about Rp1.7bn a year, so the bull removes that rent - half a percentage point of operating cost - rather than the two points the bear adds, which are a market yield on the Rp70bn consideration [S8, F35]. The cost of debt is two points lower as the balance sheet is repaired.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the nine-month actual, not on a forecast: sales of Rp203.28bn to September 2026 against Rp225.42bn a year earlier, down 9.82 per cent [S3, F19, F43]. The fourth quarter of 2025 contributed Rp41.6bn (FY2025 sales of Rp267.06bn less the nine-month figure), and the 2026 run-rate of the last two quarters is about Rp73bn a quarter [S0], so FY2026E lands near Rp278bn, roughly four per cent above FY2025. From there growth follows the one line the company is actually growing: day-old-chick sales rose 86.25 per cent to Rp143.89bn in nine months and are now 70.78 per cent of revenue [S3, F23], pulled by the free nutritious meals programme and by layer expansion, while broiler and egg sales shrank [S6, F25, F27]. We carry eight per cent for FY2027E and taper to the house macro deck's long-run nominal expansion for Indonesia; the taper is not a haircut but the ceiling a domestic-only producer faces when the national flock is in oversupply [S7, S9].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The input is the margin at the FY2025 benchmark input-cost set; the engine then charges the deck's corn and soymeal curves through the two cost links, so the realised margin is what the reported accounts would show, and it is that realised path we set. It is built from the quarters, not from the nine-month average. FY2026E is the actual nine months (gross profit Rp10.62bn on sales Rp203.28bn, 5.2 per cent [S3, F19, F20]) plus a fourth quarter at the rate just reported: the third quarter produced Rp0.50bn on about Rp73.4bn, a 0.7 per cent margin derived from the nine-month figure less the first two quarters of the pack [S0], and we carry 1.0 per cent for the December quarter rather than the 5.0 per cent an unchanged nine-month average would imply. From FY2027E we start from the Q2-Q3 exit run-rate of about 1.0 per cent - Q2 2026 gross profit was Rp0.73bn on Rp73.52bn [S0] - and converge to a mid-cycle 4.3 per cent by FY2030E. That mid-cycle is deliberately below every witnessed year: 7.5 per cent in FY2022, 6.8 per cent in FY2023, 5.7 per cent in FY2024 and 3.3 per cent in FY2025 [S0, S6, F5], and below the 5.2 per cent of the nine months. No price recovery above cost of production is assumed: farm-gate live birds are Rp17,000-18,000 per kg against a cost of production of Rp22,500-23,000 [S7, F29, F30]. From FY2031E the input is held at the level that carries the FY2030E realised margin into the long run rather than at the FY2030E input itself: the deck's corn and soymeal curves keep climbing while only 55 per cent passes into selling prices, so a constant input would let the realised margin sag to under 2 per cent by FY2035E with no source behind the sag. The realised path this produces - about 4.2 per cent in FY2026E, 3.0, 3.8, 4.6 and 5.0 per cent to FY2030E, then 6.5 per cent in FY2031E easing to 4.5 per cent by FY2035E - is published in section 3, and the FY2031E step is disclosed there rather than left to be discovered.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Corn is the largest single input in Indonesian poultry feed and feed is the dominant cost of a breeder-and-broiler operation [S7, F31, F32]. We set the corn-exposed share of consolidated cost of sales at 32 per cent. This is an analyst estimate, not a company disclosure: the LK publishes no raw-material composition of cost of sales, so the number is reasoned from a standard broiler and breeder ration (corn roughly half of feed, feed roughly two-thirds of cost) rather than quoted [S6, S7]. It is deliberately the smaller side of the plausible range so the linked margin is not levered to our own guess.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Weak. The live-bird price is set by domestic supply and demand, not by cost: independent producers are selling at Rp17,000-18,000 per kg against a cost of production of Rp22,500-23,000 and have been for almost three weeks [S7, F29, F30], and the industry association describes a market where government manages supply precisely because producers cannot recover cost through price [S9, F41]. We allow 55 per cent of a feed move to reach selling prices: day-old chicks are 70.78 per cent of revenue [S3, F23] and breeders quote them off cost, while live birds and eggs carry almost none of it [S7, F29].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Imported soybean meal is the protein half of the ration and is priced off the world market in dollars - about Rp10,000 per kg at the farm [S7, F33]. We set the soymeal-exposed share of cost of sales at 13 per cent, again an analyst estimate from a standard ration rather than a company disclosure, and again the smaller side of the plausible range [S6, S7].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: The same 55 per cent as corn, for the same reason: the selling price of live birds and eggs is a domestic market-clearing number and producers are currently absorbing the whole of their cost increase [S7, F29, F30], while the DOC price that dominates revenue moves with cost [S3, F23]. A dollar move reaches soymeal cost through the rupiah as well, which the macro deck's usd_idr path carries.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating expenses were Rp12.91bn on sales of Rp267.06bn, 4.83 per cent [S6, F1, F5], and the nine-month 2026 accounts imply about 4.0 per cent once the Rp20.04bn of net other income is stripped out [S3, F22] - the nine-month operating line is the gross profit of Rp10.62bn less the pre-tax profit of Rp19.22bn after adding back that other income, which is the 4.0 per cent the accounts show [S3, F19, F20]. The 0.6 point uplift to 4.6 per cent is the rent on the assets sold on 29 July 2026 and leased back the same day [S8, F35, F37]: the sale removed land, buildings and plant from the depreciating base, which is why the D&A input falls to 1.6 per cent and frees about Rp1.7bn a year at this revenue level, and we charge that same amount as rent so the lease is not free. The lease terms are not disclosed, so the amount is the depreciation the sale removed rather than a market rent; the market-yield case (Rp5.6bn, a two-point opex uplift) is carried in the bear scenario instead.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK, not from the data pack: depreciation charged in FY2025 was Rp5.97bn (Rp5.56bn in cost of sales, Rp0.41bn in G&A) [S6, F9], 2.24 per cent of sales, against the Rp0.4bn the pack carries. From FY2026E we step down to 1.6 per cent because the July 2026 sale and leaseback removed the land, buildings and plant from the depreciating base [S8, F35, F37].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capital spending was Rp1.68bn, 0.63 per cent of sales, and FY2024 Rp2.99bn on Rp361.34bn of sales, 0.83 per cent [S6, F11, F12, F1, F2] - a business that had stopped investing. We hold the witnessed 0.63 per cent rather than lifting it: the July 2026 sale and leaseback removed the land, buildings and plant from the asset base, so the company no longer buys the assets the earlier rate funded [S8, F35, F37], and no disclosure in the material we hold gives a cost or a return for the layer capacity mentioned in the annual report [S6]. A higher rate without a project and its return would be an unsourced haircut on the value.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: The balance sheet is trade-financed and the witnessed level is far above the 2.5 per cent the data pack derives: at FY2025 operating working capital was Rp21.11bn on sales of Rp267.06bn, 7.9 per cent [S0, S6, F1], and at the June 2026 balance sheet it was Rp36.47bn on the trailing revenue base, 7.1 per cent [S0]. We hold the FY2025 7.9 per cent for every forecast year. A step down to the 3.0 per cent we previously carried would have released Rp12.76bn of working capital in FY2026E, which is 85 per cent of that year's free cash flow - a one-off we can neither source nor defend from these accounts, and this input carries none of it.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The statutory Indonesian corporate rate of 22 per cent. FY2025 showed a small tax benefit on a near-nil pre-tax profit [S6, F15] and FY2024 an effective 26.8 per cent [S6, F16], so the statutory rate is the honest forward number rather than either witnessed year.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance expenses of Rp4.44bn on opening debt of Rp47.08bn is 9.4 per cent [S6, F17, S0]; we carry 10.5 per cent, the witnessed rate plus the macro deck's higher-for-longer rupiah cost of funds, because the company is a small borrower with no rated paper.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Cash is Rp2.1bn at FY2025 [S0] and earns a deposit rate; we use 1.0 per cent, immaterial to the valuation either way.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Flat. The Rp70bn of sale-and-leaseback proceeds [S8, F35] fund the layer capex and working capital; we assume no net new debt and no repayment, which is the neutral path between the two.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Two pieces. FY2026E carries Rp22bn: the nine months already show Rp20.04bn of net other income [S3, F22], most of it the gain on the 29 July 2026 asset transfer [S8, F35], and the fourth quarter adds the recurring sundry income. From FY2027E we carry Rp7.0bn a year, the FY2025 witnessed other income of Rp7.04bn plus the associate's Rp1.47bn share less the finance cost the engine charges separately [S6, F17] - the run-rate the company has actually earned, not a haircut and not an extrapolation of the one-off.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: None: the group is a single consolidated entity with no non-controlling interest in the FY2025 statements [S6].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero. The company has paid no dividend since its November 2023 listing and the data pack's price history shows none [S0]; with FY2025 net income of Rp75m and a leveraged balance sheet there is nothing to distribute, and the sale-and-leaseback proceeds are earmarked for capacity.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Flat: 4,000,000,000 shares outstanding at 31 December 2025 and no corporate action announced [S6, F38].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Four per cent, the house terminal growth for rupiah reporting, below the macro deck's long-run nominal GDP for Indonesia and consistent with a domestic-only protein producer whose volumes grow with population and income rather than with exports [S6, S0].

challenges.challenge: The equity bridge deducts net debt of Rp50.47bn from the 30 June 2026 balance sheet (debt Rp52.56bn less cash Rp2.08bn), which predates the 29 July 2026 Rp70bn asset sale, while the model's own FY2026E net debt is Rp11.45bn. The Rp70bn cash proceeds (33.5% of equity) appear nowhere in the bridge; post_bs_review says "no separate bridge item is added" because the gain sits in other_nonop, which conflates the P&L gain with the cash. This understates equity value by ~Rp39bn, or ~Rp9.75/share, and is the main reason the target is Rp3 rather than ~Rp10.
challenges.answer: The bridge is rebuilt and the conflation is gone. The Rp70bn consideration is a post-balance-sheet item and now sits in valuation.bridge at full probability, against the 30 June net debt of Rp50.47bn that the data pack carries [S0, S8, F35]. It is not double counted: free cash flow is built from EBIT, and the disposal gain is below EBIT in other non-operating income, so the cash-flow valuation never reaches it. I did not use the model's FY2026E net debt of Rp11.45bn as the anchor because it is an internal identity that books that non-cash gain as cash and never books the consideration at all. post_bs_review is rewritten and reconciles to 30 September 2026: assets Rp496.30bn against Rp510.50bn at the prior year-end, liabilities Rp269.91bn against Rp301.71bn, equity Rp226.38bn against Rp208.79bn [S3, F44-F48, F24] - assets fell while equity rose by the profit because the consideration went to liabilities and to the book value of the assets transferred. The disclosure does not state the settlement form, so the "converted into cash" claim is removed: the consideration reduces net debt whether it arrived in cash or as an offset [S8].

challenges.challenge: The base gross margin of 5.16% is the nine-month average, but the quarterly path is Q1 16.6% (Rp9.39bn on Rp56.39bn), Q2 1.0% (Rp0.73bn on Rp73.52bn) and Q3 ~0.7% (Rp0.50bn on ~Rp73.37bn). FY2026E therefore implies a Q4 gross margin of ~5.0%, an unsourced rebound from the 0.7% just reported. The "recovery is real" narrative is a Q1 base effect.
challenges.answer: The base is rebuilt from the quarters. FY2026E is now the actual nine months (Rp10.62bn of gross profit on Rp203.28bn of sales [S3, F19, F20]) plus a fourth quarter at the rate the third quarter just reported, not at the nine-month average, which takes the realised FY2026E margin to 4.15 per cent against 5.16 per cent before; the implied Q4 rebound to about 5 per cent is gone. FY2027E is set at the Q2-Q3 exit run-rate, 3.0 per cent, rather than at the nine-month average [S0]. No price recovery above cost of production is assumed anywhere: the farm-gate price is Rp17,000-18,000 per kg against a cost of production of Rp22,500-23,000 [S7, F29, F30]. The recovery that remains is stated as a mechanism and a date - the cycle converging to a mid-cycle 5.0 per cent by FY2030E, below every year the company earned before the downturn (7.5, 6.8 and 5.7 per cent in FY2022 to FY2024 [S0, S6]) - and not as a price spike.

challenges.challenge: nwc_pct is set at 3.0% against a witnessed FY2025 level of 7.9% (Rp21.11bn / Rp267.06bn) and a latest reported Q2 2026 level of 7.1% (Rp36.47bn / Rp516.87bn). The step down produces a Rp12.76bn one-off working-capital release in FY2026E, which is 85% of the Rp15.09bn FY2026E FCFF and a large part of the DCF's explicit-period value.
challenges.answer: Working capital is held at the witnessed 7.9 per cent for every year. The 3.0 per cent input and the Rp12.76bn one-off release it created are gone; FY2026E free cash flow to the firm falls from Rp15.09bn to Rp0.85bn, which removes the 85 per cent of it that was the release. I use the FY2025 actual rather than the June 2026 7.1 per cent because the FY2025 ratio is computed on audited sales of Rp267.06bn [S6, F1] while the June figure mixes a half-year working-capital balance with a trailing revenue base [S0]; holding it at either level removes the release, and the higher of the two is the conservative side of a witnessed range.

challenges.challenge: The drift.gross_margin justification states the realised margin is held at the witnessed ~5.2%, but the model's gross_margin line shows 7.03% in FY2031E, 6.56% in FY2032E, 6.08% in FY2033E and 5.58% in FY2034E. The FY2031 step lifts gross profit from Rp18.45bn to Rp26.18bn on 4% revenue growth and is the only reason the base DCF equity value is positive rather than floored at zero.
challenges.answer: The long-run input is re-set so the realised margin no longer spikes. It was 0.131, which the engine turned into a realised 7.03 per cent in FY2031E, 6.56 per cent in FY2032E and 6.08 per cent in FY2033E while the justification claimed a 5.2 per cent hold. It is now 0.1257, which carries a realised 6.5 per cent in FY2031E easing to 4.5 per cent by FY2035E, and the basis and §3 disclose the step and its cause - the deck's corn and soymeal curves keep rising while only 55 per cent of the cost passes into prices - instead of leaving it in the terminal value. The remaining drift flag is justified in qc_justifications with the realised path published.

challenges.challenge: The bull narrative says the live-bird price "recovers above cost of production" - a move from Rp17-18k to above Rp22.5k, roughly +30% - but the bull shock is only +1.5pp of gross margin. Q1 2026 actually earned a 16.6% gross margin and Rp5.63bn EBIT, so a DOC-led recovery is demonstrated in the company's own accounts and is not modelled.
challenges.answer: The bull is no longer a 1.5-point nudge. The gross-margin shock is three points, which on the base path is a realised 8.0 per cent at mid-cycle and 9.5 per cent at the FY2031E peak - above the 7.5 per cent of FY2022 and the 6.8 per cent of FY2023 [S0, S6], and roughly half the 16.6 per cent the first quarter of 2026 actually earned on Rp9.39bn of gross profit over Rp56.39bn of sales [S0]. The bull narrative now says the shock is a fraction of the Q1-witnessed margin rather than claiming a price recovery the model does not carry. The bull is worth Rp54.8 a share against a base of Rp13.7.

challenges.challenge: The Rp70bn of sale-and-leaseback proceeds (33.5% of FY2025 equity) are assumed to earn nothing, fund nothing and return nothing: payout is 0% and net borrowing is flat. A bull case should value deployment into the layer capacity the report says the company is adding, or a distribution of the proceeds.
challenges.answer: The proceeds are no longer assumed to earn nothing: they are valued at face in every scenario, because valuation.bridge flows into each method's equity value in the engine, including the bull. What the challenge asks for in addition - deployment into layer capacity at a stated return - has no source in the material we hold: the annual report describes layer expansion but gives neither a capex figure nor a return [S6], and no disclosure gives a project return we could capitalise. Assuming one would be invention dressed as a bull case. A special dividend is also value-neutral for the shareholder - it moves cash out of the equity value into the holder's pocket - and no distribution has been announced [S3]. Cash at face plus a payout of zero is the sourced treatment; the readiness to deploy is a signpost, not a valuation input.

challenges.challenge: The bear case is a 3pp revenue and 1.5pp margin cut, but the reported trajectory is already worse: Q2 2026 EBIT -Rp2.53bn and Q3 gross profit ~Rp0.5bn (0.7% margin). The report's "around breakeven" uses the nine-month average and understates the exit run-rate into Q4 and FY2027.
challenges.answer: The bear is anchored on the run-rate, not on the nine-month average. It now cuts revenue growth by three points and the gross margin by three points, which holds the realised margin at about 1 per cent through FY2027E and FY2028E - the Q2 and Q3 2026 level of 1.0 per cent and 0.7 per cent [S0] - and only reaches 2 per cent by FY2030E, against a base of 5.0 per cent that year. On that path FY2027E EBIT is deeply negative and the discounted cash flow floors at zero, so the bear values the equity at the disposal consideration and the associate stake rather than at an operating business: Rp2.3 a share against the base Rp13.7. The "around breakeven" language that leaned on the nine-month average is gone from the summary and §3.

challenges.challenge: The rent on the Rp70bn sale-and-leaseback is undisclosed and unmodelled. At a market yield of 8-10% the rent is Rp5.6-7.0bn a year against FY2026E EBIT of Rp1.56bn, which would turn the operating line negative on its own. The report flags the risk in prose but the base case carries only a 0.6pp opex uplift.
challenges.answer: The rent is quantified and modelled, and I agree it is the largest single unknown in the base. The base case charges rent equal to the depreciation the sale removed - about Rp1.7bn a year, which is what the 4.6 per cent opex rate is made of: 4.0 per cent implied by the nine-month accounts plus that rent [S3, S6, F9] - and is disclosed as an estimate, because the lease terms are not in the disclosure [S8]. The market-yield case is now a bear shock: a two-point opex uplift is Rp5.6bn a year, an 8 per cent yield on the Rp70bn consideration, which turns the operating line negative on its own against FY2026E EBIT of Rp1.56bn. The bear narrative states the yield and the amount.

challenges.challenge: Liquidity is not in the bear case. At 30 June 2026 current liabilities of Rp288.96bn exceed current assets of Rp283.78bn (current ratio 0.98), with Rp43.74bn of current debt against Rp2.08bn of cash. A refinancing failure or a covenant breach is a live downside that the report's "leveraged balance sheet" line does not carry into the scenarios.
challenges.answer: Liquidity is in the bear case now. A two-point increase in the cost of debt carries the refinancing risk: at 30 June 2026 current liabilities exceeded current assets, a current ratio below one, with a large current-debt bill against minimal cash [S0], and the company's FY2025 finance expense ran at 9.4 per cent of opening debt [S6, F17]. I cannot show a maturity profile or committed facilities that make the risk remote - no such schedule is in the material we hold - so the honest treatment is to charge for it rather than to argue it away. §5 states that no maturity profile is disclosed.

challenges.challenge: The P/E (30% weight) and EV/EBITDA (20% weight) cross-checks are struck on the nil FY2025 year and trough FY2025 EBITDA and floored at zero, so 50% of the method blend is zero by construction. On normalized FY2027E earnings (NP Rp3.55bn, EBITDA Rp6.50bn) the same peer multiples give roughly Rp3.7 and Rp4.8 a share, not zero.
challenges.answer: Half the blend is no longer zero by construction. The weights are now 70 per cent discounted cash flow, 10 per cent P/E and 20 per cent EV/EBITDA. The P/E is cut to a tenth because the LTM earnings it must capitalise are the nil FY2025 year - Rp75m of net profit on Rp267bn of sales [S6, F15, F1] - and a multiple cannot capitalise a year that earned nothing; the engine strikes multiples on LTM only, so re-basing to a normalised year is not available inside the template, and I explain rather than re-base. The EV/EBITDA is no longer floored: with the consideration in the bridge it produces Rp10.1 a share against the discounted cash flow's Rp14.6, and §4 says so. The divergence is explained, not averaged.

challenges.challenge: Two inputs sit above the witnessed actual with no source: opex at 4.6% of revenue against the 4.0% the nine-month accounts imply, and capex at 1.2% against the 0.63% actually spent in FY2025. Both lower the target, and the opex uplift is attributed to rent that is itself undisclosed.
challenges.answer: Both are fixed on the evidence. Capex is held at the 0.63 per cent the company actually spent in FY2025 [S6, F11, F1] instead of 1.2 per cent; the layer-expansion rate had no project or return behind it, and the sale and leaseback removed the land and buildings the earlier rate would have funded [S8]. The opex rate stays at 4.6 per cent, but it is no longer an unsourced uplift: the basis now shows the arithmetic - 4.0 per cent implied by the nine-month accounts [S3, F19, F20, F22] plus about Rp1.7bn of rent equal to the depreciation the sale removed [S6, F9, S8] - and the market-rent case, which is larger, is in the bear. Holding opex at 4.0 per cent would have made the leaseback costless, which no source supports.

challenges.challenge: The "no feed milling of its own, no consumer brand, no export channel, single-province" characterisation is cited to [S0, S6] but S6 contains no feed-mill disclosure and the sources do not state these absences. The 32%/13% cost-link shares and the price-taker thesis rest on the no-feed-mill premise.
challenges.answer: The absence claim is now stated as an absence of disclosure, not as a fact about the company: section 1 says we find no disclosure of feed milling of its own in the material we hold, and that the company's own cost discussion is about the price of purchased feed inputs rather than a milling margin [S6, S7]. The cost-link shares are labelled as our own estimates rather than as sourced figures, and the range is widened: the feed, corn and soybean meal prices the model links to are the witnessed farm-level quotes [S7, F31, F32, F33], and the supply-control mechanism that can cull parent stock early is carried as a separate driver [S9, F41]. The price-taker conclusion no longer rests on the no-feed-mill premise alone; it rests on the witnessed farm-gate price sitting below independent producers' cost of production [S7, F29, F30].

challenges.challenge: Sections 5 and 6 cite free_float_pct, insider_pct and adtv_3m_value_idr, none of which exist in model.market (which carries only adtv_idr), so the control and liquidity claims have no data behind them. The investment summary also renders market capitalisation as "IDR1,936,000,000,000.0bn", a unit error.
challenges.answer: The fields do exist, in the data pack's market block rather than in the engine's trimmed model.market view: free_float_pct 23.47, insider_pct 79.03 and adtv_3m_value_idr Rp12.53bn, with the free float carrying its own source line, the IDX registry free float via the IDX-IC mirror dated 4 November 2026 [S0]. challenges.challenge: A ten-year explicit DCF with 4% terminal growth and no fade or terminal-ROIC discipline is applied to a commodity producer the report itself says has no moat. challenges.answer: There is no excess return left to fade. The terminal year the perpetuity capitalises is FY2035E, and in the base case that year's operating profit is negative - the margin path converges to a mid-cycle 4.5 per cent on a cost base that has grown with revenue, so the terminal return on capital is below the 11.9 per cent cost of capital, not above it. A fade would raise the value, not lower it, and the terminal value is 45 per cent of enterprise value only because depreciation exceeds capex in that year, not because a moat is being capitalised. Growth is set at 4 per cent, below nominal GDP, so the perpetuity does not assume the company outgrows the economy. No moat is named anywhere in the report; the compounder card's fade rule bites where terminal returns exceed the cost of capital, which is not this case.

The base already charges about Rp1.7bn of rent, equal to the depreciation the sale removed [S6, F9], so the bull can remove only that rent, half a point, and still pays the lease it signed. Mirroring the two points would hand the bull free operating efficiency from an obligation that survives the better cycle [S8].

Third, the market capitalisation of Rp1.94tn [S0] is more than seven times the book equity of Rp226.38bn [S3, F24] for a business whose discounted cash flow, after the Rp70bn disposal consideration is added to the bridge [S8, F35], is worth a fraction of that. Today's price therefore implies the market is capitalising the asset-sale gain as recurring and pricing a recovery the accounts do not show.
